q: Which approach to perception emphasises the role of unconscious inference and probabilistic reasoning in interpreting sensory information?

concept.t: Unconscious inference is Helmholtz's idea: the brain silently works out what the sensory input most likely means.
It is the core of Gregory's constructivism, which builds the percept from the input plus what we already know.
Its probabilistic, Bayesian form treats the percept as the most likely interpretation of the evidence.

wrong.a: Marr's approach, which asks what each stage of vision computes, not how inference shapes the percept.
wrong.c: Gibson's view, the direct opposite: it denies that inference is needed at all.
wrong.d: Describes perception as a series of stages, without stressing inference.

q: According to the Bayesian approach to perception, our perceptual experiences are influenced by:

concept.t: Bayes's theorem combines two things: the prior and the likelihood.
The prior is what is likely in the world, learnt from experience or built in by evolution.
The likelihood is how well each possibility fits the current sensory evidence; the percept combines the two.

wrong.a: Genes can shape the priors, but they are not what the Bayesian definition names.
wrong.b: Culture can shape the priors, but the definition is prior beliefs plus evidence, not culture.
wrong.d: Emotion can shape the priors, but none of these is the definition.

q: Which psychologist is associated with the concept of "affordances", which refers to the opportunities for action provided by the environment?

concept.t: An affordance is what the environment offers for action: a chair affords sitting, a handle affords grasping.
Affordances are central to Gibson's ecological theory (1979).

wrong.a: An inference (top-down) theorist, on the opposite side of the debate from Gibson.
wrong.c: Another inference (top-down) theorist, like Helmholtz; affordances are not his idea.
wrong.d: Proposed the perceptual cycle, a different model; affordances are Gibson's term.

q: According to Wundt, "apperceptive mass" constitutes ___________.
who: Herbart's term, taken over by Wundt

concept.t: The apperceptive mass is the body of ideas a person already has.
A new perception is absorbed into this mass and so made meaningful: pure perception plus preexisting ideas.
The term is Herbart's; Wundt took it over.

wrong.a: Describes associationist compounds of elements, not a new perception absorbed into existing ideas.
wrong.b: Leaves out the existing ideas, which are the whole point of the mass.
wrong.d: Mixes in Helmholtz's unconscious inference, a different theory.

q: The most important school of psychology which has contributed a lot towards perception is:
who: Wertheimer, Koffka and Köhler, phi phenomenon (1912)

concept.t: Wertheimer, Koffka and Köhler began Gestalt psychology with the phi phenomenon (1912).
It gave perception figure-ground organisation, the grouping laws and Prägnanz.
That is why Gestalt psychology is the school most linked with perception.

wrong.c: Structuralism analysed sensations into elements; it did not explain how they are organised.

q: According to the law of ______, items which are close together in space and time tend to be perceived as belonging together or forming an organised group.
who: Gestalt law of proximity (Wertheimer's grouping laws)

concept.t: Proximity means nearness: items close together in space or time are grouped together.
The words close together or near in a stem signal proximity.

wrong.b: Groups elements lying on a smooth path, not nearby ones.
wrong.c: Groups elements that look alike, whatever their distance.
wrong.d: The completion of gaps in a figure.

q: The tendency to complete a figure is called:

concept.t: Closure is the tendency to complete a figure by filling in its gaps.
A circle drawn with gaps is still seen as a complete circle.

wrong.a: Another name for the law of good continuation, which is about smooth paths, not gaps.
wrong.b: Same law as continuation (good continuation): smooth paths, not gaps; two names for one law.
wrong.d: Groups look-alike elements; it does not complete figures.

q: Any figure or form not perceived in parts but organised in perception in the best possible whole form is known as:

concept.t: Prägnanz, the law of good figure or simplicity, says we see the simplest, most stable and complete organisation possible.
It is the master law; the other laws are special cases of it.

wrong.a: One particular kind of organisation (nearby items group together), a special case of Prägnanz.
wrong.c: Figure-ground describes one particular kind of organisation (an object standing out from its background), not the best-whole principle.
wrong.d: One particular kind of organisation (elements on a smooth path group together), a special case of Prägnanz.

q: Determining a rule of structure from incomplete evidence and then identifying items that fulfil the rule would be a demonstration of:

concept.t: Structuring is imposing an organising rule on incomplete input.
You then pick out the items that fit the rule, exactly what the stem describes.

wrong.a: Interpolation fills in between known points; it does not impose a rule of structure.
wrong.b: Extrapolation extends a trend beyond the known points.
wrong.c: A monocular depth cue (overlap); the trap is its similar-sounding name.

q: Among monocular cues for depth perception is:

concept.t: In interposition, an object that partly hides another is seen as nearer.
One eye is enough to see it, so it is a monocular cue.

wrong.a: One of the two binocular cues, so not monocular.
wrong.b: The other binocular cue, so not monocular.
wrong.c: Not a depth cue at all: it is Piaget's term, or the opposite of contrast.

q: Retinal disparity, which enables three-dimensional depth perception, is classified as which type of visual depth cue?

concept.t: Retinal disparity is the difference between the two eyes' images.
It needs two eyes by definition, and it gives stereopsis, so it is a binocular cue.

wrong.a: Monocular static cues are the pictorial ones; disparity needs two eyes.
wrong.c: Monocular and needs movement; disparity needs two eyes, not movement.
wrong.d: Pictorial cues are monocular and static; disparity needs two eyes.

q: Highway engineers sometimes paint stripes on freeway off-ramps to enhance the perception of depth. This uses the cue of:

concept.t: Texture normally looks more crowded with distance: the texture gradient.
Stripes that get closer together exaggerate that crowding and heighten the sense of speed.

wrong.a: Haze on distant objects; painted stripes add no haze.
wrong.b: Needs relative movement of objects at different distances, not a painted pattern.
wrong.c: Overlap is interposition, one object hiding another.

q: The density of stones increases as we look farther away. This phenomenon is due to:

concept.t: With distance, texture elements look smaller, finer and more densely packed: the texture gradient.
Stones packed more densely farther away are exactly this cue.

wrong.a: A binocular eye-muscle cue, not a property of the surface.

q: What is the approximate visual field covered by each human eye?
who: Visual field of one eye, as keyed

concept.t: Choose 180 degrees for this exact item, as the paper keys it.
Be careful: the better textbook figure for one eye is about 160 degrees horizontally, about 60 degrees towards the nose and 100 towards the temple.
180 to 200 degrees is the field of both eyes together, with about 120 degrees of binocular overlap; recognise 160 if a question is precise about a single eye.

wrong.a: Smaller than the standard figures; one eye covers about 160 degrees.
wrong.b: The more accurate textbook figure for one eye, but not the keyed answer; choose it when a question is precise about a single eye.
wrong.d: More than even the 180 to 200 degrees covered by both eyes together.

q: When you stretch your right hand farther away from your body, you still perceive it to be of the same size as your left hand. This is due to:

concept.t: The far hand's retinal image is smaller.
The brain scales it by distance (size-distance invariance), so the hand still looks its true size: size constancy.

wrong.c: A depth cue from movement, not a constancy.
wrong.d: What size constancy uses, not the name of the effect.

q: Illusions are:

concept.t: An illusion is a misinterpretation of stimuli arising from a real external object.
Real object, wrong reading: illusion. No adequate external stimulus: hallucination.

wrong.b: What Sims calls a sensory distortion, such as micropsia.
wrong.d: The definition of a hallucination.

q: Illusions are:

concept.t: In an illusion, a real stimulus is misperceived.
A hallucination has no adequate external stimulus.

wrong.b: A hallucination has no adequate external stimulus, while an illusion starts from a real one.
wrong.c: Culture and learning shape susceptibility, as the carpentered-world studies show, so not purely innate.
wrong.d: Describes a hallucination; an illusion starts from a real stimulus.

q: Optical illusions result from distortion in:

concept.t: In the Müller-Lyer figure the retinal image is accurate and the receptors transduce it correctly.
The error lies in the interpretation, which is perception.

wrong.b: Sensation works normally; the input is registered correctly.
wrong.d: Sensory adaptation works normally and is not the source of the error.

q: The rail tracks appearing to converge to all of us is an example of:

concept.t: Illusions are classed as personal or permanent (universal).
An illusion that everyone experiences every time is permanent, as with converging rail tracks; answer as keyed.
The convergence itself is the depth cue of linear perspective.

wrong.b: Varies between people and occasions, such as a rope seen as a snake.
wrong.c: Broadly true, but the item is testing the personal versus permanent classification.
wrong.d: A different, specific illusion; converging tracks are not the Müller-Lyer figure.

q: It has been found that the Müller-Lyer illusion exists in certain cultures in which there are:
who: Segall, Campbell and Herskovits, carpentered world (1963, 1966)

concept.t: The carpentered-world hypothesis comes from Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1963, 1966).
Experience of rectangular buildings teaches people to read angles as corners in depth, increasing susceptibility.

wrong.a: Trees are irrelevant to the hypothesis.
wrong.c: The reverse: people living among round huts and few straight edges were less susceptible.
wrong.d: The sex ratio is irrelevant.

q: The Müller-Lyer illusion is best explained by:

concept.t: Gregory (1963) argued that the fins and arrowheads are read as inside and outside corners.
So one shaft is coded as farther away and scaled up: misapplied size constancy.

wrong.b: The illusion works with one eye and on a flat page, which rules out disparity.
wrong.c: Lateral inhibition explains Mach bands and the Hermann grid.
wrong.d: Figure-ground reversal is Rubin's vase, a different phenomenon.

q: Déjà entendu refers to:

concept.t: Entendu means heard, so déjà entendu is the illusion of having heard something before.
Déjà vu is the seeing version.

wrong.b: Hypermnesia, an unusually clear memory of past events.
wrong.d: A speech disorder such as palilalia.

q: Who demonstrated that economic deprivation affects perception?

concept.t: In Bruner and Goodman's 1947 coin study, ten-year-olds judged the sizes of coins.
Poor children overestimated coin sizes more than rich children did, so economic deprivation affects perception.

wrong.a: Indian psychologists who are not associated with this classic finding.
wrong.c: A carpentered-world researcher, who studied culture and illusions.
wrong.d: Segall's fellow carpentered-world researcher, who studied culture and illusions, not deprivation.

q: The procedure called "semantic priming" is used to study which of the following phenomena?

concept.t: In semantic priming, masked primes too brief to be consciously seen come before related words.
They still speed responses to related words (Marcel, 1983), showing processing without awareness: subliminal perception.

wrong.a: Measured by d-prime in yes/no detection tasks.
wrong.c: Measured by Witkin's rod-and-frame and embedded figures tests.
wrong.d: Rotter's concept, measured by personality questionnaires.

q: What term describes the phenomenon where individuals fail to notice significant changes in their environment, even when those changes are obvious?

concept.t: Change blindness is failing to notice changes, typically when they coincide with a blink, cut or flicker.
The stem stresses failing to notice changes; that is the clue (Chapter 5).

wrong.b: Failing to see an unexpected object while attending to something else; the close trap.
wrong.c: The stable perception of objects despite changing input.
wrong.d: The focusing of processing on some stimuli rather than others.
